space-0.title: Black Knight satellite (legend, incl. 1998 STS-88 photo)
space-0.summary: Contested legend, not an established object. Claimed by UFO conspiracy writers to be an alien satellite that has orbited Earth for about 13,000 years. The story stitches together unrelated items: radio signals Nikola Tesla reported in 1899, long-delayed radio echoes first heard in 1928, Donald Keyhoe’s 1954 claim that the US Air Force had detected two satellites, a 1960 "dark object" tracked by the US Navy, Duncan Lunan’s 1973 speculation that the echoes came from a 13,000-year-old probe, and photos taken during the 1998 STS-88 Space Shuttle mission. Mainstream explanation: NASA catalogues the STS-88 photo as space debris, and space journalist James Oberg identifies it as a thermal blanket lost during the mission; the 1960 object was confirmed as the remains of a stray Discoverer 8 satellite, and Tesla’s signals have been attributed to natural sources such as pulsars.
evidence: NASA photographs from STS-88 (December 1998) show the object.
1960: Time magazine reported the Navy’s "dark object"; a follow-up confirmed it was Discoverer 8 remains.

space-1.title: STS-48 "zig-zag" lights video
space-1.place: Low Earth orbit, Space Shuttle Discovery (no ground location)
space-1.summary: Contested. Video from Space Shuttle Discovery’s cameras on STS-48 shows a point of light drifting near Earth’s horizon that appears to turn sharply after a bright flash, while other lights move away. UFO researchers have claimed it shows craft reacting to the flash. Mainstream explanation: astronaut Ron Parise and space analyst James Oberg concluded the "object" was an ice particle near the shuttle whose path was changed by a thruster firing (the flash); NASA and astronomer Phil Plait agree.
evidence: NASA video from the STS-48 mission (September 1991).

space-2.title: STS-75 tether "swarm" footage
space-2.place: Low Earth orbit, Space Shuttle Columbia (no ground location)
space-2.summary: Contested. On 25 February 1996 the Tethered Satellite System’s tether broke during deployment from Space Shuttle Columbia. Later footage of the drifting tether shows many small disc-like lights moving around it, which some ufologists claim are UFOs. Mainstream explanation: NASA says the lights are misidentified debris close to the camera; skeptics note that objects that far away would have to be enormous and visible from the ground.
evidence: NASA video of the severed tether (February 1996).

space-3.title: Gemini 4: McDivitt’s cylindrical object
space-3.summary: Astronaut Jim McDivitt reported a "white cylindrical shape with a white pole sticking out of one corner" and took two pictures; his crewmate was asleep. McDivitt himself says it was unknown but man-made debris, not alien. Space analyst James Oberg argues it was most likely the mission’s own Titan II second stage. Claimed by ufologists as an astronaut UFO sighting.

space-4.title: Gemini 7 "bogey"
space-4.summary: Frank Borman radioed "We have a bogey at ten o’clock high" and said it was an actual sighting, then described "millions" of particles. Ufologists later claimed it as a UFO. Mainstream explanation: James Oberg’s trajectory analysis points to debris around the spent booster, and Borman himself later confirmed that what he saw was not a UFO.

space-5.place: Earth orbit / re-entry, Voskhod 2 (no ground location)
space-5.summary: Rumors circulated that cosmonauts Alexei Leonov and Pavel Belyayev saw an unidentified cylindrical object around re-entry on the mission that made the first spacewalk. space-6.title: Apollo 11 "light alongside" (Aldrin)
space-6.place: Between Earth and the Moon (no ground location)
space-6.summary: Buzz Aldrin said he "observed a light out the window that appeared alongside" the spacecraft on the way to the Moon, and says his 2005 interview was taken out of context by UFO promoters. Stories that Neil Armstrong saw glowing orbs or alien craft trace back partly to a hoax by science-fiction writer Otto Binder. Mainstream explanation: jettisoned spacecraft components travelling near Apollo 11.

space-7.title: Skylab 3 bright reddish object
space-7.summary: The Skylab 3 crew watched a "bright reddish object", brighter than Jupiter, pulsing about every 10 seconds for some 10 minutes until it entered Earth’s shadow, and photographed it. Astronaut Owen Garriott said it was "obviously a satellite in a very similar orbit". Contested: optical physicist and ufologist Bruce Maccabee argued a satellite did not fit; James Oberg answered that it was likely debris and that odd details in the best photo are artifacts.

space-8.title: STS-80 "F1 Event" and lights
space-8.place: Over the Atlantic near the Puerto Rico Trench (apparent source of the streak)
space-8.summary: Contested. Shuttle cameras on STS-80 recorded a circle of lights and a fast streak dubbed the "F1 Event". James Oberg and mission astronaut Tom Jones say ice particles or debris drifting near Columbia explain the footage. Marine scientist Edwin Alfonso-Sosa and engineer Mark Carlotto argued the F1 streak does not fit the ice explanation. In 2026 three STS-80 photos released in the Pentagon UFO files were labelled "unresolved".
evidence: 2026 Pentagon release: three photos marked unresolved.

space-10.title: ISS live-feed and crew "UFO" clips
space-10.place: International Space Station (no fixed ground location)
space-10.summary: Clips from the station’s public camera feeds are often shared as UFOs. In 2016 a bright object appeared just before the feed cut out, and it was claimed NASA cut the feed on purpose. Other cases: a 2013 object near a Progress cargo ship, and a 2020 cosmonaut time-lapse of the aurora with "space guests". Mainstream explanation: NASA says the feed drops automatically when the station loses its relay-satellite link, and that reflections, the Moon, debris and Earth lights cause most "objects"; the 2013 object was an antenna cover from the Zvezda module, and the cosmonaut later said his objects seemed to be satellites.
evidence: NASA statement (2016): feed loss is automatic during relay-satellite gaps.

space-11.title: Wow! signal
space-11.place: Received at Big Ear radio telescope, Delaware, Ohio, USA (source: deep space, toward Sagittarius)
space-11.summary: A strong narrowband radio signal recorded by Ohio State University’s Big Ear telescope for its full 72-second observing window. Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the printout and wrote "Wow!". It has never been detected again. Some researchers suggest it could have been an extraterrestrial transmission. A 2017 claim that comets caused it is discredited; a 2024 preprint proposed a rare natural event in which a cold hydrogen cloud suddenly brightened.

space-12.title: ʻOumuamua (first known interstellar object)
space-12.place: Discovered with Pan-STARRS, Haleakalā, Hawaii, USA (object was ~33 million km away)
space-12.summary: The first interstellar object seen passing through the Solar System: very elongated, reddish and tumbling, it sped up slightly in a way gravity alone does not explain. Contested: Avi Loeb and Shmuel Bialy proposed it might be an artificial solar sail; other scientists say the evidence does not support that. Mainstream explanations are natural, such as outgassing of hydrogen or nitrogen ice; its make-up remains unknown.
evidence: Radio searches (Green Bank, Allen Telescope Array) found no signals.

space-14.title: Vela incident (double flash)
space-14.place: Near the Prince Edward Islands, Indian Ocean
space-14.summary: A US Vela satellite recorded a double flash of light characteristic of a nuclear explosion. Contested for decades: it is widely believed to have been an undeclared nuclear test, but this has never been officially confirmed; the US Department of Defense initially suggested a mix of phenomena such as lightning and a meteoroid hitting the satellite, and a White House-convened expert panel re-examined the data.

space-15.title: Tabby’s Star dimming
space-15.place: Star KIC 8462852 in Cygnus, seen by the Kepler space telescope (pin position illustrative)
